query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled isothermal annealing at Tg − 5 K for 2 hours will induce a glass-to-glass transition that enhances the thermal stability of a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Rapidly quenched amorphous phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy (e.g., Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) initially in a high-energy, less-relaxed state.
generation.intervention: Immediately following quenching, subject the alloy to an annealing treatment held isothermally at Tg − 5 K for 2 hours under an inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: The annealing must be performed in a controlled inert environment with temperature precision of ±2 K to avoid crossing Tg, ensuring only relaxation occurs without triggering crystallization.
generation.structural_mediator: The thermal treatment facilitates atomic rearrangements that reduce free volume and relax internal stresses, transitioning the alloy into a denser, low-energy amorphous state.
generation.mechanism: By promoting structural relaxation below Tg, the treatment reduces the potential energy of the amorphous phase, thereby raising the crystallization onset temperature and improving thermal stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable increase in the crystallization onset temperature (by approximately 20 K) and a broader, more stable supercooled liquid region relative to as-quenched samples.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus-containing amorphous alloy produced by rapid quenching with no subsequent annealing treatment.
generation.boundary: The annealing temperature must remain narrowly below Tg to prevent premature crystallization; deviations may lead to either insufficient relaxation or the onset of crystallization.
generation.uncertainty: Low to moderate uncertainty due to well-established relaxation phenomena in amorphous materials, though exact temperature sensitivity may vary with composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of amorphous samples from the same melt-spun batch. Subject one set to isothermal annealing at Tg − 5 K for 2 hours while keeping the other as quenched. Analyze differences through DSC and mechanical testing.
measurements: DSC to compare crystallization onset temperatures and the width of the supercooled liquid region
Nanoindentation or other mechanical tests to assess changes in thermal/mechanical stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase (e.g., >15–20 K) in crystallization onset temperature and improved thermal stability compared to the unannealed ones, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractGlass-to-glass transitions are useful for us to understand the glass nature, but it remains difficult to tune the metallic glass into significantly different glass states. Here, we have demonstrated that the high-entropy can enhance the degree of disorder in an equiatomic high-entropy metallic glass NbNiZrTiCo and elevate it to a high-energy glass state. An unusual glass-to-glass phase transition is discovered during heating with an enormous heat release even larger than that of the following crystallization at higher temperatures. Dramatic atomic rearrangement with a short- and medium-range ordering is revealed by in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction analyses. This glass-to-glass transition leads to a significant improvement in the modulus, hardness, and thermal stability, all of which could promote their applications. Based on the proposed high-entropy effect, two high-entropy metallic glasses are developed and they show similar glass-to-glass transitions. These findings uncover a high-entropy effect in metallic glasses and create a pathway for tuning the glass states and properties.Subject terms: Glasses, Metals and alloys Glass-to-glass transitions can help understandi

papers.title: Thermal and Structural Analysis of a High-Entropy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 Alloy-Infl
papers.approach: Experimental study of solidification and crystallization under various cooling regimes (slow cooling on a copper plate, rapid cooling via electric arc pulse, and melt‐spinning) to probe phase evolution and amorphization.
papers.findings: Phosphorus in the alloy dramatically broadens the solidification temperature range and modifies crystallization; slow cooling produces multiple crystalline phases while rapid cooling (especially via melt-spinning) enables the formation of a predominantly amorphous phase. The addition of phosphorus is shown to lower effective solidification temperatures and promote undercooling needed for glass formation.
papers.mechanism: Phosphorus is proposed to promote the formation of phosphide-rich or phosphorus-modified phases, thereby reducing the liquidus temperature of phosphorus-poor phases and enhancing undercooling. This interferes with crystal nucleation and growth, favoring amorphization under rapid cooling.

papers.title: Designing High Entropy Bulk Metallic Glass (HE-BMG) by Similar Element Substitution/Addition
papers.system: High-entropy bulk metallic glasses (HE-BMGs) such as Ti20Hf20Cu20Ni20Be20 and Ti16.7Zr16.7Nb16.7Cu16.7Ni16.7Be16.7
papers.approach: Composition engineering via similar element substitution/addition to adjust atomic size distribution and lattice distortion in HEAs, thereby influencing the liquidus temperature and glass-forming ability.
papers.findings: Substitution of elements (e.g., replacing Zr with Hf) and addition of elements (e.g., Nb) can lower the liquidus temperature and modify parameters such as the reduced glass transition temperature and the supercooled liquid region. A lower liquidus temperature, in turn, is closely associated with improved glass-forming ability. However, adjustments may trade off with factors like ductility or thermal stability.
papers.mechanism: By manipulating the degree of lattice distortion (quantified via parameters such as δ′), similar element substitution alters atomic packing density and reduces the driving force for crystallization. Lowering the liquidus temperature enhances undercooling during rapid processing, thereby stabilizing the amorphous phase.

papers.title: Predictive Modeling of High-Entropy Alloys and Amorphous Metallic Alloys Using Machine Learning.
papers.system: Various metallic glasses and HEAs characterized by diverse compositions
papers.approach: Computational and machine learning based modeling to correlate thermodynamic parameters (e.g., enthalpy of mixing, atomic size mismatch) and the glass-forming ability.
papers.findings: The models suggest that alloys with more exothermic mixing (negative ΔH) and significant atomic radius mismatch exhibit improved glass-forming ability. Parameters like increased viscosity from atomic mismatches and lowered liquidus temperatures are key for stabilizing the amorphous state.
papers.mechanism: Increased atomic heterogeneity and lower liquidus temperatures hinder atomic rearrangement and crystal nucleation, promoting amorphization under rapid cooling conditions.

papers.title: Exploring the Phase Space of Multi-Principal-Element Alloys and Predicting the Formation of Bulk Metallic Glasses.
papers.system: Multi-principal-element alloys including Pd-Ni-P based systems and Ti-Zr-Cu-Ni system
papers.approach: Computational exploration and micro-alloying studies to map the glass-forming composition space and calculate the critical cooling rates required for amorphization.
papers.findings: For Pd-Ni-P alloys, micro-alloying with elements of similar atomic size (Co, Cu, Fe) had little influence on the glass-forming ability, whereas elements with larger differences (Gd) significantly altered the critical cooling rate. The approach confirms that both compositional tuning and processing kinetics must be controlled to obtain the amorphous phase.
papers.mechanism: Minor changes in atomic size mismatches and the resulting modifications in liquid viscosity and nucleation barriers influence both the kinetic and thermodynamic pathways for glass formation.

established: Phosphorus addition in high-entropy alloys broadens the solidification range and promotes glass formation under rapid cooling.
Lowering the liquidus temperature enhances the undercooling necessary to bypass crystallization, improving glass-forming ability.
High mixing entropy and significant atomic size mismatches contribute to increased viscosity and hinder atom rearrangement, both favoring amorphization.

approaches_tried.approach: Varying cooling rates (slow cooling, rapid cooling via electric arc pulse, and melt-spinning)
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that very rapid cooling can lead to the formation of an amorphous structure in phosphorus-containing HEAs. (PMC11642357)

approaches_tried.approach: Similar element substitution/addition (e.g., replacing Zr with Hf, adding Nb)
approaches_tried.outcome: Shown to adjust the liquidus temperature and lattice distortion, thereby affecting the glass-forming ability and altering thermal stability parameters. (PMC8911233)

In some glass-forming systems, micro-alloying with elements of similar size had little effect on GFA, whereas elements with significant atomic differences (e.g., Gd in Pd-Ni-P) produced measurable changes. (PMC7516748)

mechanisms: Phosphorus lowers the crystallization (liquidus) temperature by promoting phosphide formation and expanding the solidification range, increasing undercooling.
High entropy contributes to sluggish diffusion, which kinetically retards crystallization and aids in the stabilization of the amorphous phase.
Atomic size mismatch increases viscosity and causes lattice distortion, both of which impede crystalline nucleation and growth.
disagreements: While phosphorus addition is generally beneficial for glass formation, some reports hint that it may reduce ductility or affect other mechanical properties adversely.
The effect of high entropy is not uniformly positive; for some compositions, the improvement in GFA via high mixing entropy is counterbalanced by an increase in the liquidus temperature.
open_questions: What is the optimum compositional tweak (beyond phosphorus addition) that will lower the liquidus temperature while preserving or enhancing the amorphous state’s thermal stability?
How can minor substitutions or additions be combined with phosphorus to achieve a balance between improved glass-forming ability and mechanical performance?
What are the quantitative relationships between phosphorus content, cooling rate, and the onset of crystallization in these complex alloy systems?
opportunities: Investigate a combined intervention that leverages targeted similar element substitution (e.g., using a minor addition of an element that forms phosphide phases or has a favorable atomic radius) to further lower the liquidus temperature in phosphorus-containing HEAs.

Conduct systematic studies varying both phosphorus content and selected substitution elements under controlled rapid cooling to quantitatively assess improvements in GFA and amorphous thermal stability.
Utilize machine learning models to predict optimal compositional adjustments that synergize with phosphorus’s role, enabling the design of alloys with enhanced amorphous phase stability.

directions.direction: Micro-alloying with a minor addition of a large atomic radius element (e.g., Gd).
directions.assessment: Directly targets the reduction of the liquidus temperature by enhancing atomic size mismatch and forming phosphide complexes. Literature indicates that even minute additions (on the order of 1 at%) can markedly shift critical cooling rates (PMC7516748::web::013::3_3_micro_alloying), making this intervention both feasible and informative.

directions.direction: Micro-alloying with a minor addition of Nb.
directions.assessment: Aims to modify the lattice distortion (δ′ parameter) to suppress crystallization. Some evidence suggests Nb may adjust the liquidus temperature (PMC8911233::web::012::5_conclusions), though reports are mixed (PMC8911233::web::006::4_1_glass_forming_ability_gfa_of_high_en), making the approach promising yet with moderate risk.

This post-quench treatment induces a glass-to-glass transition from a high-energy to a low-energy state, thereby improving thermal stability. Previous studies (PMC9023469::web::019::4_discussion) support the concept, while the intervention is highly controllable.

directions.direction: Application of ultrasonic vibration during rapid quenching.
directions.assessment: Ultrasonic agitation can homogenize the melt and disrupt nascent nuclei, promoting more uniform vitrification. Though not directly evidenced in the provided phosphorus‐containing systems, underlying physics and related studies on melt treatment suggest feasibility and potential for significant improvement.

directions.direction: Similar-element substitution to fine-tune lattice distortion.
directions.assessment: Involves replacing a constituent with a similar element that has a slightly different atomic radius to enhance local disorder. Prior work (PMC8911233::web::010::4_2_atomic_radius_characteristics_of_he_) indicates that even subtle adjustments in atomic size distribution can affect the glass-forming ability, though the approach may require fine compositional control.

candidates.intervention: Incorporate 1 at% Gd into the alloy during synthesis by adjusting the melt composition.

candidates.hypothesis: A minor addition (≈1 at%) of niobium (Nb) to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy will improve glass-forming ability and thermal stability by fine-tuning lattice distortion.
candidates.intervention: Incorporate 1 at% Nb during alloy synthesis to slightly alter the overall atomic size distribution.

candidates.hypothesis: Integrating ultrasonic vibration (≈20 kHz) during the rapid quenching process of a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy will enhance its glass-forming ability and thermal stability by reducing heterogeneous nucleation.
candidates.intervention: Apply continuous ultrasonic vibration at approximately 20 kHz during the rapid quenching (e.g., melt-spinning) process.
